claim: Tuberculosis claims more human lives than any other bacterial infection.
source: Tuberculosis (TB), is a major threat to global health as it claims more human lives than any other bacterial infection (Chakaya et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chakaya et al., 2021

claim: The emergence of multi- and extensively drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis has limited capability to fight tuberculosis.
source: The emergence of multi- and extensively drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), the bacterium that causes TB, has further limited our capability to fight the disease.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the introduction

claim: Poor compliance with prolonged treatment regimens is one major factor contributing to the emergence of drug-resistant TB.
source: One major factor contributing to the emergence of drug-resistant TB is poor compliance with prolonged treatment regimens.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: A subset of M.tb bacterial population defined as 'persisters' tolerate TB drugs.
source: While combinatorial drug therapy kills the majority of M.tb bacilli, a subset of the bacterial population, defined as 'persisters', tolerate TB drugs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the introduction

claim: The persister subset of M.tb requires prolonged treatment for sterilization to occur.
source: This persister subset requires prolonged treatment for sterilization to occur (Gideon and Flynn, 2011; Lillebaek et al., 2002; Peddireddy et al., 2017; Wayne and Hayes, 1996).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Mechanisms of persistence in M.tb are likely multifactorial, involving cell wall peptidoglycan remodelling, transporters or efflux pumps, and alternative energy sources.
source: Mechanisms of persistence in M.tb are likely multifactorial, involving cell wall peptidoglycan (PG) remodelling, transporters or efflux pumps, and alternative energy sources (Keren et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Keren et al., 2011 and Zhang et al., 2012

claim: PG is an essential component of the bacterial cell wall and constitutes the exoskeleton of bacterial cells.
source: PG is an essential component of the bacterial cell wall and constitutes the exoskeleton of bacterial cells.
evidence: Stated as established scientific knowledge

claim: PG consists of long glycan chains composed of N-acetyl muramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine that are cross-linked via stem peptide chains.
source: PG consist of long glycan chains composed of two different sugars N-acetyl muramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine that are crossed linked via stem peptide chains.
evidence: Stated as established scientific knowledge about PG structure

claim: The PG composition of M.tb in slowly replicating states is likely distinct from that during active growth.
source: The PG composition of M.tb in slowly replicating states is likely to be distinct from the one during active growth (Gupta et al., 2010; Schoonmaker et al., 2014; Wietzerbin et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gupta et al., 2010; Schoonmaker et al., 2014; Wietzerbin et al., 1974

claim: A high percentage of peptide crosslinks in M.tb join the third amino acids (3–3 linkages) of adjacent stem peptides instead of classical 4–3 linkages.
source: In particular, a high percentage of peptide crosslinks in M.tb join the third amino acids (3–3 linkages) of the adjacent stem peptides instead of the classical 4–3 linkages, and these linkages are formed by transpeptidases (Tolufashe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tolufashe et al., 2020

claim: The 4–3 linkages are generated by D,D-transpeptidases (also known as penicillin-binding proteins).
source: The 4–3 linkages, which were historically considered to predominate throughout bacterial growth and senescence, are generated by a well-known enzyme class, namely the D,D-transpeptidases (also known as penicillin-binding proteins) (Tolufashe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tolufashe et al., 2020

claim: The 3–3 linkages are generated by L,D-transpeptidases.
source: The 3–3 linkages are generated by the more recently discovered enzyme class, the L,D-transpeptidases (Mainardi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mainardi et al., 2005

claim: M.tb strain lacking the gene encoding LdtMt2 exhibits attenuation in virulence.
source: LdtMt2 plays an important role since an M.tb strain lacking the gene encoding this enzyme exhibits attenuation in virulence and exhibits enhanced susceptibility to β-lactam antibiotics (Bianchet et al., 2017; Brammer Basta et al., 2015; Dubée et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2010; Libreros-Zúñiga et al., 2019; Sanders et al., 2014; Schoonmaker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: M.tb strain lacking the gene encoding LdtMt2 exhibits enhanced susceptibility to β-lactam antibiotics.
source: LdtMt2 plays an important role since an M.tb strain lacking the gene encoding this enzyme exhibits attenuation in virulence and exhibits enhanced susceptibility to β-lactam antibiotics (Bianchet et al., 2017; Brammer Basta et al., 2015; Dubée et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2010; Libreros-Zúñiga et al., 2019; Sanders et al., 2014; Schoonmaker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Loss of function of LdtMt1 is associated with altered and attenuated cellular physiology of M.tb.
source: Additional reports have demonstrated altered and attenuated cellular physiology of M.tb in association with the loss of function of LdtMt1 (Schoonmaker et al., 2014) and LdtMt5 (Brammer Basta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoonmaker et al., 2014

claim: Loss of function of LdtMt5 is associated with altered and attenuated cellular physiology of M.tb.
source: Additional reports have demonstrated altered and attenuated cellular physiology of M.tb in association with the loss of function of LdtMt1 (Schoonmaker et al., 2014) and LdtMt5 (Brammer Basta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brammer Basta et al., 2015

claim: L,D-transpeptidases are inhibited by the carbapenem subclass of β-lactam drugs.
source: The requirement of L,D-transpeptidases for virulence has suggested that they may comprise valuable drug targets, and indeed these enzymes are inhibited by the carbapenem subclass of β-lactam drugs (Mainardi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mainardi et al., 2005

claim: Carbapenems are efficacious against both dividing and non-dividing mycobacteria.
source: Recent work further suggests the efficacy of these carbapenems against both dividing and non-dividing mycobacteria (Hugonnet et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hugonnet et al., 2009

claim: Crystal structures of L,D-transpeptidases bound to carbapenems such as meropenem, tebipenem, biapenem, and faropenem have been described.
source: To further evaluate the druggability of the L,D-transpeptidases class, several independent groups have described the crystal structures of this enzyme class bound to carbapenems such as meropenem, tebipenem, biapenem, and faropenem (Bianchet et al., 2017; Erdemli et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Steiner et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The biochemical mechanisms and kinetics of inhibition of L,D-transpeptidases by β-lactams have been documented.
source: The biochemical mechanisms and kinetics of inhibition of L,D-transpeptidases by β-lactams have been documented (Cordillot et al., 2013), and new experimental β-lactams that target M.tb L,D-transpeptidases have recently been described (Bianchet et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cordillot et al., 2013

claim: New experimental β-lactams that target M.tb L,D-transpeptidases have been described.
source: The biochemical mechanisms and kinetics of inhibition of L,D-transpeptidases by β-lactams have been documented (Cordillot et al., 2013), and new experimental β-lactams that target M.tb L,D-transpeptidases have recently been described (Bianchet et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bianchet et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2021

claim: The L,D-transpeptidase class in M.tb is comprised of at least four substructural domains including two immunoglobulin-like domains (IgD1 and IgD2), a YkuD domain, and a C-terminal subdomain (CTSD).
source: The L,D-transpeptidase class in M.tb is comprised of at least four substructural domains including two immunoglobulin-like domains (IgD1 and IgD2), a YkuD domain, and a C-terminal subdomain (CTSD).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about L,D-transpeptidase structure

claim: The YkuD domain plays a role in catalytic function and β-lactam binding.
source: The YkuD domain is known to play a role in catalytic function and β-lactam binding (Erdemli et al., 2012), while the roles of the other domains remain less certain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Erdemli et al., 2012

claim: The YkuD domain has a highly conserved motif HXX14-17[S/T]HGChN containing three residues analogous to the catalytic triad of cysteine proteases.
source: The YkuD domain has a highly conserved motif HXX14-17[S/T]HGChN containing three residues analogous to the catalytic triad of cysteine proteases: a cysteine, a histidine and a third residue (Cysteine 354, Histidine 336, and Serine 337 in LdtMt2) to catalyse the transpeptidation reaction (Erdemli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erdemli et al., 2012

claim: The catalytic triad in LdtMt2 consists of Cysteine 354, Histidine 336, and Serine 337.
source: The YkuD domain has a highly conserved motif HXX14-17[S/T]HGChN containing three residues analogous to the catalytic triad of cysteine proteases: a cysteine, a histidine and a third residue (Cysteine 354, Histidine 336, and Serine 337 in LdtMt2) to catalyse the transpeptidation reaction (Erdemli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erdemli et al., 2012

claim: The catalytic triad residues reside under a flap formed by a long loop.
source: This catalytic triad residues resides under a flap formed by a long loop.
evidence: Stated as established structural knowledge

claim: The flap can open and close to create two cavities (the inner and outer cavities) around a cysteine residue that are connected by a narrow tunnel.
source: The flap can open and close to create two cavities (the inner and outer cavities), around a cysteine residue, that are connected by a narrow tunnel (Fakhar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fakhar et al., 2017

claim: The inner and outer cavities are binding sites for the acyl acceptor and acyl donor tetrapeptide stems.
source: It is proposed that these cavities are binding sites for the acyl acceptor and acyl donor tetrapeptide stems (L-alanyl-D-Glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanine) with the donor tetrapeptide binding to the outer cavity and the acceptor tetrapeptide to the inner cavity (Erdemli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erdemli et al., 2012

claim: Several carbapenems bind both the inner and outer cavities to form covalent linkage with catalytic cysteine residue of L,D-transpeptidases.
source: As the β-lactam class of drugs mimics the tetrapeptide stems of PG, several of the carbapenems have been found to bind both the inner and outer cavities to form covalent linkage with catalytic cysteine residue of the L,D-transpeptidases (Bianchet et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bianchet et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2017

claim: The disaccharide-tetrapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanine is the substrate for L,D-transpeptidases.
source: The disaccharide-tetrapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanine is the substrate for L,D-transpeptidases (Cordillot et al., 2013; Lavollay et al., 2008) while the D,D-transpeptidases use the disaccharide-pentapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanyl-D-alanine as their substrate (Tolufashe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cordillot et al., 2013; Lavollay et al., 2008

claim: D,D-transpeptidases use the disaccharide-pentapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanyl-D-alanine as their substrate.
source: The disaccharide-tetrapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanine is the substrate for L,D-transpeptidases (Cordillot et al., 2013; Lavollay et al., 2008) while the D,D-transpeptidases use the disaccharide-pentapeptide N-acetylglucosamine-N-acetylmuramic acid-L-alanyl-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelyl-D-alanyl-D-alanine as their substrate (Tolufashe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tolufashe et al., 2020

claim: Interactions between the peptide subunits of nascent PG substrates with their relevant enzymes have been described.
source: Interactions between the peptide subunits of these nascent PG substrates with their relevant enzymes have been described (Cordillot et al., 2013; Erdemli et al., 2012; Fakhar et al., 2017; Lavollay et al., 2008; Mainardi et al., 2005), and it is generally assumed that the disaccharide component of the subunit interacts only with transglycosylases (Fibriansah et al., 2012; Mavrici et al., 2014) and thus are not relevant to the transpeptidases.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: It is generally assumed that the disaccharide component of PG substrates interacts only with transglycosylases and not with transpeptidases.
source: Interactions between the peptide subunits of these nascent PG substrates with their relevant enzymes have been described (Cordillot et al., 2013; Erdemli et al., 2012; Fakhar et al., 2017; Lavollay et al., 2008; Mainardi et al., 2005), and it is generally assumed that the disaccharide component of the subunit interacts only with transglycosylases (Fibriansah et al., 2012; Mavrici et al., 2014) and thus are not relevant to the transpeptidases.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fibriansah et al., 2012; Mavrici et al., 2014

claim: Studies with Bacillus subtilis L,D-transpeptidase LdtBs have suggested binding of the disaccharide component through a PG recognition domain, LysM.
source: Recent studies with the Bacillus subtilis L,D-transpeptidase LdtBs have suggested binding of the disaccharide component through a PG recognition domain, LysM, within LdtBs (Schanda et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schanda et al., 2014

claim: The LysM domain is absent in M.tb L,D-transpeptidases.
source: However, the mechanism of PG recognition may be different in M.tb since this LysM domain is absent in its L,D-transpeptidases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about M.tb L,D-transpeptidases

claim: The crystal structure of LdtMt2 was solved at 1.57 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure of LdtMt2 was solved at 1.57 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: Experimental data from this study as shown in Table 1

claim: An electron density was identified in a pocket between the IgD2-YkuD domains, and a glucose molecule could be modelled into the electron density at 1.0 sigma.
source: This high-resolution crystal structure is an improvement of our previous efforts (Erdemli et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2017) that enabled us to identify an electron density in a pocket between the IgD2-YkuD domains, and a glucose molecule could be modelled into the electron density at 1.0 sigma (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental crystallographic data from this study shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The glucose molecule identified in the crystal structure is likely part of a PG disaccharide moiety originating from E. coli cell lysate during LdtMt2 purification.
source: This glucose molecule is likely to be part of a PG disaccharide moiety originating from the E. coli cell lysate during LdtMt2 purification.
evidence: Inference based on the source of the protein and the identity of the molecule

claim: The sugar molecule is ensconced at the IgD2-YkuD domain interface in a pocket making several electrostatic interactions with residues R209, E207, E168, R371, Y330, and A171.
source: The sugar molecule is ensconced at the IgD2-YkuD domain interface in a pocket, which we referred to as the S-pocket, making several electrostatic interactions with residues R209, E207, E168, R371, Y330, and A171.
evidence: Experimental crystallographic data from this study

claim: Three residues M157, A171, and L391 stabilize the sugar through hydrophobic interactions.
source: Three residues M157, A171, and L391 stabilize the sugar through hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: Experimental crystallographic data from this study

claim: A higher molar concentration of N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanyl-D-isoglutamine gradually shifted the melting curve of LdtMt2 indicative of saturable binding behaviour.
source: A higher molar concentration of N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanyl-D-isoglutamine gradually shifted the melting curve of LdtMt2 indicative of saturable binding behaviour (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental ThermoFluor assay data from this study shown in Figure 1B, C

claim: R209E and E207A mutations in the S-pocket disrupted the binding of N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanyl-D-isoglutamine with LdtMt2.
source: R209E and E207A mutations in the S-pocket disrupted the binding of N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanyl-D-isoglutamine with LdtMt2.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and binding data from this study

claim: Y330F mutation affected the binding of PG precursor.
source: Y330F mutation also affected the binding of PG precursor.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and binding data from this study

claim: The order of magnitude of detrimental effect of mutations in the S-pocket on PG precursor binding is R209E ≥ E207A > Y330.
source: This was the order of magnitude of detrimental effect of mutations in the S-pocket on PG precursor binding: R209E ≥ E207A > Y330.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and binding data from this study

claim: The binding of PG precursor with the S-pocket was in mM range, indicating weak binding.
source: As the binding of PG precursor was in mM range, this indicated a weak binding with the S-pocket.
evidence: Inference from experimental binding data

claim: Superposition of LdtMt2–sugar complex with LdtBS–PG complex suggests that longer nascent PG chains thread across the S-pocket in between the IgD1-YkuD domains of LdtMt2.
source: Superposition of the structures of the LdtMt2–sugar complex with the LdtBS–PG complex suggests that longer nascent PG chains thread across the S-pocket in between the IgD1-YkuD domains of LdtMt2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Structural comparison and modeling shown in Figure 1D

claim: In the LdtBS structure, the acidic sugar moieties of PG chain bind in-between the LsyM domain and catalytic domain across a positively charged groove.
source: In the LdtBS structure, the acidic sugar moieties of PG chain bind in-between the LsyM domain and catalytic domain across a positively charged groove (Figure 1E).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: A PG chain was computationally placed over a positively charged surface across the IgD2-YkuD domain interface encompassing the S-pocket.
source: Based on the structural details of PG binding in LdtBS (Schanda et al., 2014) and LdtMt2 (Figure 1A), a PG chain was computationally placed over a positively charged surface across the IgD2-YkuD domain interface encompassing the S-pocket.
evidence: Computational modeling based on structural data

claim: Computational modelling of a longer PG chain spatially aligns one of its tetrapeptide stem across an inner cavity of the catalytic site in YkuD domain in LdtMt2.
source: This computational modelling of a longer PG chain spatially aligns one of its tetrapeptide stem across an inner cavity of the catalytic site in YkuD domain in LdtMt2 (Figure 1E), similar to reports of carbapenem and a PG-moiety binding in the same position (Bianchet et al., 2017; Erdemli et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Computational modeling shown in Figure 1E and supported by citations

claim: The inner cavity of the catalytic site is proposed to bind the acceptor tetrapeptide stem, and the outer cavity to bind the donor tetrapeptide stem prior to their 3–3 transpeptide cross-linkage by LdtMt2.
source: This inner cavity of the catalytic site is proposed to bind the acceptor tetrapeptide stem, and the outer cavity to bind the donor tetrapeptide stem prior to their 3–3 transpeptide cross-linkage by LdtMt2 (Erdemli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erdemli et al., 2012

claim: The S-pocket anchors the disaccharide moiety of one of the nascent PG chains prior to transpeptidation of tetrapeptide stems in the catalytic site.
source: Based on our crystal structure and modelling study, we propose that the S-pocket anchors the disaccharide moiety of one of the nascent PG chains prior to transpeptidation of tetrapeptide stems in the catalytic site.
evidence: Inference from crystal structure and modeling data

claim: The full-length LdtMt2 holoenzyme showed a Vmax of 0.23 µM/min and Km of 16.32 µM in the nitrocefin hydrolysis assay.
source: The full-length LdtMt2 holoenzyme showed a Vmax of 0.23 µM/min and Km of 16.32 µM in the nitrocefin hydrolysis assay (Table 2).
evidence: Experimental kinetic data from this study shown in Table 2

claim: Deletion of the IgD1 domain assessed by the IgD2-YkuD domain fragment resulted in no effect on the β-lactam hydrolysis.
source: Deletion of the IgD1 domain assessed by the IgD2-YkuD domain fragment resulted in no effect on the β-lactam hydrolysis.
evidence: Experimental data from domain deletion studies

claim: Deletion of IgD2 from the YkuD domain led to a significant adverse effect on the nitrocefin hydrolysis activity with an increase in the Km value to 129 µM (an ~eightfold increase) and a decline in enzyme turn-over by ~tenfold.
source: However, deletion of IgD2 from the YkuD domain as assessed by the YkuD fragment alone led to a significant adverse effect on the nitrocefin hydrolysis activity with an increase in the Km value to 129 µM (an ~eightfold increase) and a decline in enzyme turn-over by ~tenfold (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1, and Table 2).
evidence: Experimental data from domain deletion studies shown in Figure 2B and Table 2

claim: The S-pocket plays an important role in governing the catalytic activity of LdtMt2 enzyme.
source: This suggests an important role of S-pocket which is partly carried by the IgD2 domain in governing the catalytic activity of LdtMt2 enzyme.
evidence: Inference from experimental domain deletion and mutagenesis data

claim: Y330F mutation led to a decrease in the nitrocefin hydrolysis with a Vmax 0.15 µM/min and Km of 11.12 µM.
source: Y330F mutation led to a decrease in the nitrocefin hydrolysis with a Vmax 0.15 µM/min and Km of 11.12 µM.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and kinetic data from this study

claim: R209E mutant hydrolysed nitrocefin with a Km 428 µM that is ~26-fold higher than wild-type, while its Vmax remained almost the same as wild-type.
source: R209E mutant hydrolysed nitrocefin with a Km 428 µM that is ~26-fold higher than wild-type, while its Vmax remained almost the same as wild-type.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and kinetic data from this study

claim: E207A mutation showed a decrease in the β-lactam hydrolysis activity as compared to wild-type.
source: A E207A mutation also showed a decrease in the β-lactam hydrolysis activity as compared to wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: R209E mutation did not cause major changes in the secondary structure content of LdtMt2 enzyme as assessed by circular dichroism spectroscopy.
source: We ruled out any impact of R209E mutation on the secondary structure content of LdtMt2 enzyme using circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The CD spectra of wild-type and R209E mutant show overall similar folds.
source: In fact, an overall good overlapping CD spectrum of the wild-type and the R209E mutant suggests that the proteins maintain an overall similar folds.
evidence: Experimental CD spectroscopy data

claim: ThermoFluor assay suggests no major difference in the thermal melting of R209E and wild-type, indicating no major changes in overall fold of the protein.
source: Our biophysical ThermoFluor assay also suggests no major difference in the thermal melting of R209E and wild-type, indicating no major changes in overall fold of the protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental ThermoFluor assay data shown in Figure 1C

claim: After 200 ns of MD simulations, structural and conformational changes were observed in the catalytic center of YkuD domain including the catalytic triad residues C354, H336, and S337 and other residues in the catalytic site.
source: After 200 ns of MD simulations, structural and conformational changes were observed in the catalytic center of YkuD domain including the catalytic triad residues C354, H336, and S337 and other residues in the catalytic site, namely, S351, M303, and W340.
evidence: Computational MD simulation data from this study

claim: After MD simulations in wild-type LdtMt2, H336-NE2 formed a hydrogen bond interaction with side chain hydroxyl group oxygen (OG) of S351.
source: After the MD simulations in wild-type LdtMt2, H336-NE2 formed a hydrogen bond interaction with side chain hydroxyl group oxygen (OG) of S351 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Computational MD simulation data shown in Figure 3A

claim: A hydrogen bond interaction was observed between H336-ND1 and backbone oxygen (O) of S337 in wild-type LdtMt2.
source: A hydrogen bond interaction was also observed between H336-ND1 and backbone oxygen (O) of S337 (Figure 3A), and this interaction has been reported to be important for stabilizing the tautomer of H336 protonated at NE2 (Erdemli et al., 2012).
evidence: Computational MD simulation data shown in Figure 3A and supported by citation

claim: In the MD simulated structure of the R209E mutant, the imidazole ring of H336 was flipped leading to disruption of hydrogen bond interaction between H336-ND1 and backbone oxygen (O) of S337.
source: When we assessed the MD simulated structure of the R209E mutant, we found that imidazole ring of H336 was flipped that led to a disruption of hydrogen bond interaction between H336-ND1 and backbone oxygen (O) of S337 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Computational MD simulation data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In R209E mutant, no hydrogen bond interaction was found between H336-NE2 and the hydroxyl group oxygen (OG) of the S351 residue.
source: In addition, no hydrogen bond interaction was found between H336-NE2 and the hydroxyl group oxygen (OG) of the S351 residue and a probably density graph calculated between H336-NE2 and S351-OG pair also computed an increase in their distance during 200 ns of simulations (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Computational MD simulation data shown in Figure 3B

claim: W340 residue comes closer to M303 and H336 through hydrophobic interactions to block the outer pocket of catalytic core in R209E mutant.
source: Another W340 residue that resides outside the catalytic pocket comes closer to M303 and H336 through hydrophobic interactions to block the outer pocket of catalytic core.
evidence: Computational MD simulation data

claim: Blockage of outer catalytic pocket by W340 would hinder the dynamics of the YkuD flap.
source: Such blockage of outer catalytic pocket by W340 would also hinder the dynamics of the YkuD flap, which has been reported to be important in β-lactam binding (Fakhar et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from MD simulation data and supported by citation to Fakhar et al., 2017

claim: R209E mutation led to an increase in the fluctuations of a loop that interacts with S351 residue.
source: Notably, R209E mutation led to these major changes in the fluctuations in LdtMt2: (1) an increase in the fluctuations of a loop that interacts with S351 residue, (2) a decrease in the fluctuations of YkuD flap, and (3) a decrease in the fluctuations in the catalytic center.
evidence: Computational RMSF analysis from MD simulations

claim: R209E mutation led to a decrease in the fluctuations of YkuD flap.
source: Notably, R209E mutation led to these major changes in the fluctuations in LdtMt2: (1) an increase in the fluctuations of a loop that interacts with S351 residue, (2) a decrease in the fluctuations of YkuD flap, and (3) a decrease in the fluctuations in the catalytic center.
evidence: Computational RMSF analysis from MD simulations

claim: R209E mutation led to a decrease in the fluctuations in the catalytic center.
source: Notably, R209E mutation led to these major changes in the fluctuations in LdtMt2: (1) an increase in the fluctuations of a loop that interacts with S351 residue, (2) a decrease in the fluctuations of YkuD flap, and (3) a decrease in the fluctuations in the catalytic center.
evidence: Computational RMSF analysis from MD simulations

claim: K282A mutation led to a decrease in the enzymatic activity with a Vmax 0.16 µM/min and Km ~ 12 µM.
source: And indeed, a K282A mutation led to a decrease in the enzymatic activity with a Vmax 0.16 µM/min and Km ~ 12 µM (Table 2).
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis and kinetic data shown in Table 2

claim: R209E mutation impacts the fluctuations and dynamics of YkuD flap over the catalytic site.
source: These findings suggest that R209E mutation impacts the fluctuations and dynamics of YkuD flap over the catalytic site.
evidence: Inference from MD simulation data

claim: Two major allosteric modulations in LdtMt2 can be regulated by S-pocket: (1) modulation of S351 residue via K282 to stabilize H336-NE2 in the catalytic site; (2) modulation of YkuD flap dynamics via Y330, Q327, D304, S306, and H330 to impact the catalysis.
source: Based on the dynamic distance analysis, we propose two major allosteric modulations in LdtMt2 that can be regulated by S-pocket: (1) modulation of S351 residue via K282 to stabilize H336-NE2 in the catalytic site; (2) modulation of YkuD flap dynamics via Y330, Q327, D304, S306, and H330 to impact the catalysis.
evidence: Inference from MD simulation and dynamic distance analysis

claim: R209E mutation in the S-pocket impacts both allosteric modulations to slow down the catalysis.
source: We suggest that R209E mutation in the S-pocket impacts both of these allosteric modulations to slow down the catalysis, as seen in nitrocefin hydrolysis assay (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inference from MD simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutation of catalytic triad residue S337 to alanine did not disrupt the β-lactam hydrolysis activity.
source: Mutation of catalytic triad residue S337 to alanine did not disrupt the β-lactam hydrolysis activity and this is expected as a S337A mutation should not disrupt the hydrogen bond interaction between H336-ND1 and backbone oxygen of alanine residue.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis data

claim: Mutation of C354 to alanine and H336 to asparagine disrupted β-lactam hydrolysis.
source: Mutation of C354 to alanine and H336 to asparagine disrupted β-lactam hydrolysis as expected.
evidence: Experimental mutagenesis data

claim: Mutation of the S351 residue to alanine disrupted β-lactam hydrolysis activity, almost to the same degree as seen in the H336N mutant, with a ~15-fold decrease in enzyme turn-over.

claim: Penicillin and cephalosporin subclasses are readily hydrolysed by LdtMt2.

evidence: Stated as established knowledge

source: Mutation of catalytic residues C354, H336, and S351 also abrogated acylation with biapenem.

claim: Both the S-pocket and the catalytic center play important roles in driving acylation of the C354 catalytic residue by biapenem.
source: These findings suggest that both the S-pocket and the catalytic center play important roles in driving acylation of the C354 catalytic residue by biapenem.

claim: Increasing concentrations of biapenem led to a gradual change in melting temperature of LdtMt2 until it was fully saturated.

claim: Biapenem binding decreased the melting temperature of LdtMt2 protein.

claim: E207A and Y330F mutations showed detrimental effect on saturable behaviour of biapenem.
source: E207A and Y330F mutations also showed detrimental effect on saturable behaviour of biapenem.

claim: The order of magnitude of detrimental effect of mutations in the S-pocket on reversible biapenem binding is R209E > E207A > Y330.

claim: Mutations in the S-pocket hindered both non-covalent as well as covalent interactions with biapenem.

claim: Varying concentrations of biapenem with the catalytic site mutants C354A, H336N, and S351A did not induce any further significant thermal shift, indicative of negligible or insignificant physical binding of biapenem.

claim: Mutations in catalytic site disrupt both non-covalent as well as covalent binding of biapenem to LdtMt2.

claim: Biapenem has two modes of binding: (1) covalent binding and (2) saturable, non-covalent binding.
source: From the experimental results with the wild-type, S-pocket mutants and catalytic site mutants (Figure 4), we conclude that biapenem has two modes of binding: (1) covalent binding and (2) saturable, non-covalent binding.

claim: Covalent binding of biapenem occurs at the catalytic site.
source: As covalent binding is well known at the catalytic site, saturable reversible binding seems to be at the S-pocket.

claim: Saturable reversible binding of biapenem occurs at the S-pocket.
source: As covalent binding is well known at the catalytic site, saturable reversible binding seems to be at the S-pocket.

claim: In both biapenem-binding modes, there is a cooperative role between S-pocket and the catalytic site, as mutations in any of the sites disrupt the binding.
source: In both of the biapenem-binding modes, our data suggest a cooperative role between S-pocket and the catalytic site, as mutations in any of the sites disrupt the binding (Figure 4A, C).

claim: Biapenem docked well within the S-pocket through its pyrazolo[1,2a][1,2,4]triazolium R3 group with a docking score of −6.3 kcal/mol.

claim: When biapenem molecules were docked in both the S-pocket and catalytic site simultaneously, the pyrazolo[1,2a][1,2,4]triazolium R3 group of biapenem remained ensconced in S-pocket for 0–6 ns, made hydrophobic interactions with Y330 and L391 at 7–15 ns, and its pyrrolidine ring made additional π–π interactions with Y330 at 18–28 ns while remaining in the S-pocket, before finally moving out towards the YkuD flap of the catalytic site after 40 ns.
source: However, when biapenem molecules were docked in both the S-pocket and catalytic site simultaneously, the pyrazolo[1,2a][1,2,4]triazolium R3 group of biapenem remained ensconced in S-pocket for 0–6 ns, made hydrophobic interactions with Y330 and L391 at 7–15 ns, and its pyrrolidine ring made additional π–π interactions with Y330 at 18–28 ns while remaining in the S-pocket, before finally moving out towards the YkuD flap of the catalytic site after 40 ns (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Ampicillin docked into the S-pocket with a docking score of −7.1 kcal/mol with its R1 group tail 2-amino-2-phenylacetyl ensconced in the S-pocket.

claim: All L,D-transpeptidase paralogs in M.tb (LdtMt1, LdtMt2, LdtMt3, LdtMt5) contain a pocket similar to the S-pocket found in LdtMt2.

claim: Corresponding to the R209 residue position in LdtMt2 S-pocket, LdtMt1 has R25, LdtMt3 has Q66, and LdtMt5 has H219, and each of these putative S-pocket amino acids have similar basic charge properties.
source: Corresponding to the R209 residue position in LdtMt2 S-pocket, LdtMt1 has R25, LdtMt3 has Q66, and LdtMt5 has H219, and each of these putative S-pocket amino acids have similar basic charge properties (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: A common S-pocket-mediated allosteric mechanism exists in all of the L,D-transpeptidases in M.tb.

claim: Prior to the 3–3 transpeptidation between the donor and acceptor PG stem peptides, the acceptor PG sugar moiety chain is anchored across the IgD1-YkuD domains interface to the S-pocket of LdtMt2.
source: Based on our crystal structure and modelling studies, we propose that prior to the 3–3 transpeptidation between the donor and acceptor PG stem peptides, the acceptor PG sugar moiety chain is anchored across the IgD1-YkuD domains interface to the S-pocket of LdtMt2.
evidence: Inference from crystal structure and modeling studies

claim: Upon anchoring of the PG sugar moiety chain within the S-pocket in LdtMt2, its acceptor stem peptide binds to the inner pocket of the enzyme's catalytic domain, and the donor stem binds to the outer cavity close to the C354 residue.
source: Upon anchoring of the PG sugar moiety chain within the S-pocket in LdtMt2, its acceptor stem peptide binds to the inner pocket of the enzyme's catalytic domain, and the donor stem binds to the outer cavity close to the C354 residue, interactions that foster formation of the 3–3 transpeptide linkage (Bianchet et al., 2017; Erdemli et al., 2012; Fakhar et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference from crystal structure and modeling studies, supported by citations

claim: Prior to 3–3 transpeptide linkage, both S-pocket and catalytic site may work in cooperativity to facilitate synchronous binding of two PG substrates (donor and acceptor substrates).
source: We hypothesize that, prior to 3–3 transpeptide linkage, both S-pocket and catalytic site may work in cooperativity to facilitate synchronous binding of two PG substrates (donor and acceptor substrates); however, this requires experimental validation using nascent PG substrates that are beyond the scope of our study.
evidence: Hypothesis based on inference from data, acknowledged as requiring further validation

claim: Both the S-pocket and the catalytic site regulate β-lactam hydrolysis and inhibition by the carbapenem subclass.
source: Our findings reveal the role of both the S-pocket and the catalytic site in regulating β-lactam hydrolysis and inhibition by the carbapenem subclass.
evidence: Inference from experimental data in this study

claim: There is allosteric cooperativity between the S-pocket and the catalytic site in the dual recognition of carbapenem drugs.
source: We demonstrate an allosteric cooperativity between the S-pocket and the catalytic site in the dual recognition of carbapenem drugs, with the former one binding the carbapenem drug non-covalently with a saturable binding and the latter one covalently through irreversible acylation of C354.
evidence: Inference from experimental data in this study

claim: During the β-lactam-binding process, LdtMt2 occupies one molecule of β-lactam at a reversible binding site (the S-pocket) 21 Å away from the catalytic site, and this interaction stimulates allosteric conformational changes across the YkuD catalytic flap and catalytic site to drive acylation by a second ß-lactam molecule in the catalytic pocket.
source: During the β-lactam-binding process, LdtMt2 occupies one molecule of β-lactam at a reversible binding site (the S-pocket) 21 Å away from the catalytic site, and this interaction stimulates allosteric conformational changes across the YkuD catalytic flap and catalytic site to drive acylation by a second ß-lactam molecule in the catalytic pocket.
evidence: Inference from experimental and computational data in this study

claim: The role of catalytic site is important in stimulating reversible binding of β-lactam in the S-pocket.
source: We find the role of catalytic site equally important in stimulating reversible binding of β-lactam in the S-pocket.
evidence: Inference from experimental data in this study

claim: There is bidirectional cooperativity between the S-pocket and the catalytic site in binding dual β-lactams.
source: Thus, there we observe bidirectional cooperativity between the S-pocket and the catalytic site in binding dual β-lactams, and the same mechanism may apply to dual PG substrate binding.
evidence: Inference from experimental data in this study

claim: Various β-lactams bind to the S-pocket of LdtMt2 through their tail regions, either through their R1 or R3 groups.
source: We find that various β-lactams bind to the S-pocket of LdtMt2 through their tail regions, either through their R1 or R3 groups.
evidence: Inference from docking and experimental data in this study

claim: The interactions of R1 or R3 groups with the S-pocket play critical role in the initiation of S-pocket binding, irrespective of fate of β-lactams in catalytic site.
source: As we found the docking scores of ampicillin, oxacillin, and cefotaxime to be higher than those of carbapenems, biapenem, and T203, the interactions of these R1 or R3 groups with the S-pocket appears to play critical role in the initiation of S-pocket binding, irrespective of fate of β-lactams in catalytic site.
evidence: Inference from docking data in this study

claim: The discovery of a novel mechanism of β-lactam binding in LdtMt2 reveals important new parameters in the development of new β-lactams for M. tb.
source: This discovery of a novel mechanism of β-lactam binding in LdtMt2 reveals important new parameters in the development of new β-lactams for M. tb, and highlights the importance of the respective R1 and R3 side chains to both occupy the S-pocket and modulate strong inhibition at the catalytic site.
evidence: Inference from findings in this study

claim: The study provides a high-resolution crystal structure of LdtMt2 with an experimental carbapenem T203 that offers the basis for cooperative binding of dual β-lactams in the S-pocket and catalytic site.
source: This study provides a high-resolution crystal structure of LdtMt2 with an experimental carbapenem T203 that offers the basis for cooperative binding of dual β-lactams in the S-pocket and catalytic site (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Experimental crystallographic data from this study shown in Videos 1 and 2

claim: An allosteric site at a distance of 21 Å from the catalytic site binds the sugar moiety of PG substrates (the S-pocket).
source: Here, we report identification of an allosteric site at a distance of 21 Å from the catalytic site that binds the sugar moiety of PG substrates (hereafter referred to as the S-pocket).
evidence: Experimental crystallographic and binding data from this study

claim: The S-pocket also binds a second β-lactam molecule and influences binding at the catalytic site.
source: This site also binds a second β-lactam molecule and influences binding at the catalytic site.
evidence: Experimental binding and mutagenesis data from this study

claim: Two β-lactam molecules bind co-operatively to LdtMt2, one non-covalently at the S-pocket and one covalently at the catalytic site.
source: We provide evidence that two β-lactam molecules bind co-operatively to this enzyme, one non-covalently at the S-pocket and one covalently at the catalytic site.
evidence: Experimental binding, acylation, and structural data from this study

claim: This dual β-lactam-binding phenomenon is previously unknown.
source: This dual β-lactam-binding phenomenon is previously unknown and is an observation that may offer novel approaches for the structure-based design of new drugs against M. tuberculosis.
evidence: Stated as a novel finding from this study

claim: L,D-transpeptidase function predominates in atypical 3 → 3 transpeptide networking of peptidoglycan layer in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: L,D-transpeptidase function predominates in atypical 3 → 3 transpeptide networking of peptidoglycan (PG) layer in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Prior studies of L,D-transpeptidases have identified only the catalytic site that binds to peptide moiety of the PG substrate or β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Prior studies of L,D-transpeptidases have identified only the catalytic site that binds to peptide moiety of the PG substrate or β-lactam antibiotics.
